title: Liberty and Prosperity -- Ch. 31: Yuchengco v. Sandiganbayan: Ownership of Sequestered PLDT Shares
primary_topics: Chapter 31 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' -- a digest of Yuchengco v. Sandiganbayan, in which the Court, through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales, held that the Sandiganbayan had grossly misappreciated the evidence and that the preponderance clearly lay with the Republic in its claim to the sequestered PLDT shares.

The evidentiary standard and its application: under Executive Order No. 14-A the degree of proof was preponderance of evidence, so the anti-graft court was to determine, in the light of common human experience, which of the parties' theories was more worthy of credence.

The finding on ownership: the testimonies of Jose Yao Campos, Rolando C. Gapud and Francisco de Guzman established that Prime Holdings, Inc. was organized for and owned by Marcos, so the 111,415 PTIC shares it held bore the character of ill-gotten wealth whether in the hands of Marcos or of Cojuangco.

The separate opinions: Justice Callejo's concurrence on the conclusiveness of Campos's judicial admissions against interest, and the Dissents of Justices Garcia and Sandoval-Gutierrez, who found the Republic's proof insufficient and the Cojuangcos the beneficial owners from the start.
sub_topics: Civil Case No. 0002 was filed by the Republic through the PCGG to recover the ill-gotten wealth of the late President Ferdinand E. Marcos, among the identified properties being PTIC shares held by Ramon U. Cojuangco, Imelda O. Cojuangco and Prime Holdings, Inc.
PTIC was the biggest stockholder of PLDT, holding over two million shares representing some 28 percent of the outstanding shares when the case was filed.
Alfonso T. Yuchengco and Y Realty Corporation intervened, claiming to be the rightful owners of PHI's 46 percent shareholding in PTIC.

On the Cojuangcos' Motion the Sandiganbayan severed the PLDT ownership issue and allowed a separate trial, in the course of which three consolidated Petitions were filed: the Yuchengcos challenged the denial of their Motions to suspend trial pending discovery and the declaration that they had waived the right to present evidence, and the Republic assailed the denial of additional time to complete its evidence.

With no restraining order issued, the Sandiganbayan promulgated a Partial Decision on May 6, 2002 dismissing both the Republic's Complaint and the Yuchengcos' Complaint-in-Intervention, which was in turn challenged in two further Petitions.

The interlocutory Petitions were denied for mootness or for failure to show grave abuse of discretion, and the Yuchengcos' challenge to the Partial Decision was denied for absence of reversible error, leaving as the sole issue whether that Decision conformed to the evidence, the law and settled jurisprudence.

Under Executive Order No. 14-A the required degree of proof was preponderance of evidence, not proof beyond reasonable doubt, and the court was to weigh which theory was more worthy of credence in the light of common human experience.

Jose Yao Campos, a former crony who surrendered substantial assets after the February 1986 EDSA Revolution, testified that he had organized companies for and on behalf of Marcos, one of which was PHI, whose stockholders held no financial interest and executed a Deed of Trust or Assignment in favor of an unnamed beneficiary, the original going to the President.

Rolando C. Gapud, one of the incorporators, corroborated Campos and established that PHI was a dummy corporation of the Marcoses, while former corporate secretary Francisco de Guzman confirmed that PHI had been completely organized by Campos's associates, that its office was inside United Laboratories, and that no stock certificates were issued -- only deeds of assignment.
There was hardly any evidence that the company was beneficially owned by Cojuangco, so the Court ruled that Marcos owned PHI and that all the incorporators acted under his direction.

From that premise the Court drew its conclusions: Cojuangco became president and took over management in 1981 with the cooperation of the Marcos nominees, managed the Marcos-controlled corporation for at least two years, and the 1983 simultaneous divestment by the remaining incorporators in favor of his close relatives was made with the knowledge and authorization of Marcos.

Cojuangco was therefore either one of the nominees -- like Gapud, whom he had replaced as president -- or at the very least a close associate of the late President, so the PCGG could and must recover the 111,415 PTIC shares for the Republic.

Invoking PCGG v. Peña, which described the Marcos rule as a well-entrenched plundering regime of twenty years and spoke of the magnitude of its organized pillage, the Court said the evidence revealed one more instance of that grand scheme and that it had before it an opportunity to undo, even if only to a limited extent, the damage done.

Justice Callejo concurred separately, arguing that the Republic's witnesses deserved great probative weight, that Campos's admissions were judicial and conclusive on him and his successors-in-interest, that they were admissions against interest and trustworthy, and that the acquisition of the shares had no juridical effect for want of any consideration.

Justice Garcia dissented, explaining the dismissals of the interlocutory Petitions -- mootness after the Partial Decision, no grave abuse where the parties had agreed to the trial dates and wasted them with innumerable requests for resetting, and no reversible error in granting summary judgment where no genuine issue of material fact remained.

He recounted Yuchengco's claim that the Marcos regime had coerced him into surrendering six percent of PTIC and into not exercising a 'put and call' option with General Telephone and Electronics, but found no substantial proof of coercion in the depositions, and noted Mercado-Ferrer's testimony that the 'put' option had expired in 1972 and that Y Realty had waived its preemptive right in 1978.

On the merits Justice Garcia believed the shares were not ill-gotten: Campos never declared that the deeds or blank stock certificates delivered to Marcos included PHI's, Gapud said he had assigned his shares for a consideration and had no personal knowledge of PTIC holdings, and because the deeds named their transferees rather than being indorsed in blank there was a departure from the set pattern of Marcos corporations.

Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez joined that Dissent, finding the Marcos modus operandi absent in PHI's case, calling Campos's claim never to have discussed PHI with the President contrary to human experience, and concluding that Cojuangco -- not Marcos -- had been the beneficial owner from the start, which was why the deeds were not in blank but named the Cojuangcos.

She also noted the debate over Baseco, the majority saying the Court had never intended to lay down evidentiary standards there, the Dissent noting that in Baseco the blank-indorsed certificates were found among Marcos's possessions in Malacañang while here no such documents existed.

stances.claim: The degree of proof in this case was preponderance of evidence under Executive Order No. 14-A, so the Sandiganbayan was not to look for proof beyond reasonable doubt but to determine, in the light of common human experience, which of the parties' theories was more worthy of credence.
stances.rhetorical_move: resetting the evidentiary standard at the outset, so that the sufficiency of the Republic's proof is judged by the right measure

stances.claim: The Sandiganbayan grossly misappreciated the facts and committed reversible error, because the testimonies of Campos, Gapud and De Guzman established that Prime Holdings was organized for and owned by Marcos while hardly any evidence supported beneficial ownership by Cojuangco.
stances.rhetorical_move: witness-by-witness accumulation, each one corroborating the last, set against the near-absence of contrary proof

stances.claim: The 111,415 PTIC shares held by PHI bore the character of ill-gotten wealth whether they were in the hands of Marcos or of Cojuangco, since Cojuangco was either one of the nominees or at the very least a close associate of the late President, so the PCGG could and must recover them for the Republic.
stances.rhetorical_move: inference from a chain of circumstances -- the takeover with the nominees' cooperation, the two years of management, and the authorized 1983 divestment to close relatives

stances.claim: Concurring, Justice Callejo maintained that Campos's admissions were judicial and thus conclusive on him and his successors-in-interest, that as admissions against interest they were trustworthy, and that the transfer of the PHI shares had no juridical effect because no consideration was shown for it.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidentiary reinforcement, converting testimony into binding admissions and then attacking the transfer for want of consideration

stances.claim: Dissenting, Justice Garcia held that the Republic had failed to prove that the disputed PLDT shares belonged to the Marcos family, stressing that Campos never declared the deeds delivered to Marcos included PHI's, that Gapud had assigned his shares for consideration and knew nothing of PTIC holdings, and that the deeds named their transferees instead of being indorsed in blank -- a departure from the set pattern of Marcos corporations.
stances.rhetorical_move: pattern argument run in reverse, using the absence of the familiar modus operandi as affirmative proof of a legitimate transaction

stances.claim: Joining that Dissent, Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez concluded that Cojuangco, not Marcos, had been the beneficial owner of the shares from the start, that the deeds named the Cojuangcos precisely because that was the fact, and that Campos's claim never to have discussed PHI with the President was contrary to human experience only if PHI had been one of his dummy corporations.
stances.rhetorical_move: offering an alternative 'realistic scenario' that explains the same documents more simply

notable_anecdotes: The stake was extraordinary: PTIC was the biggest stockholder of PLDT, holding over two million shares -- some 28 percent of the outstanding shares -- when Civil Case No. 0002 was filed.

Jose Yao Campos, a former crony who surrendered substantial assets to the government after the February 1986 EDSA Revolution, testified that he had organized companies for Marcos whose stockholders held no financial interest and signed deeds in favor of an unnamed beneficiary, the originals going to the President himself.

A former corporate secretary revealed that Prime Holdings kept its office inside United Laboratories, a Campos family corporation, and that the company never issued stock certificates at all -- only deeds of assignment.
The whole dispute between majority and minority turned on a matter of form: whether the deeds had been left blank, as in the familiar Marcos pattern, or named the Cojuangcos, as these ones did.

Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez contrasted the case with Baseco, where blank-indorsed stock certificates had been found among Marcos's possessions in Malacañang, while here no such documents were ever in his hands.

The Court closed its ruling on a note of historical purpose, quoting PCGG v. Peña on a well-entrenched plundering regime of twenty years and saying it had an opportunity to undo, even if only to a limited extent, the damage that had been done.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 31 of 'Liberty and Prosperity' digests Yuchengco v. Sandiganbayan, the fight over sequestered PLDT shares. The Republic, through the PCGG, had sued in Civil Case No. 0002 to recover the ill-gotten wealth of the late President Ferdinand E. Marcos, including PTIC shares held by Ramon and Imelda Cojuangco and by Prime Holdings, Inc.; PTIC was PLDT's biggest stockholder, holding some 28 percent of its outstanding shares. Alfonso T. Yuchengco and Y Realty intervened as claimants to PHI's 46 percent of PTIC. After the Sandiganbayan severed the ownership issue for separate trial and, with no restraining order in force, promulgated a Partial Decision on May 6, 2002 dismissing both the Republic's Complaint and the Complaint-in-Intervention, five consolidated Petitions reached the Court, which denied the interlocutory ones for mootness or absence of grave abuse and the Yuchengcos' for lack of reversible error, leaving only whether the Partial Decision conformed to the evidence and the law. Holding that Executive Order No. 14-A required only preponderance of evidence, the Court through Justice Conchita Carpio Morales found that the preponderance clearly lay with the Republic and that the Sandiganbayan had grossly misappreciated the facts. Jose Yao Campos testified that he had organized PHI for Marcos with stockholders who held no financial interest; Rolando C. Gapud called it a dummy corporation of the Marcoses; and Francisco de Guzman confirmed that Campos's associates had organized it, that its office sat inside United Laboratories, and that it issued only deeds of assignment. From these the Court concluded that Marcos owned PHI, that Cojuangco managed a Marcos-controlled corporation for at least two years, and that the 1983 divestment to his relatives was authorized by Marcos, so the 111,415 PTIC shares were ill-gotten in whosever hands. Justice Callejo concurred separately on the conclusiveness of Campos's admissions against interest, while Justices Garcia and Sandoval-Gutierrez dissented, holding the Republic's proof insufficient and reasoning that because the deeds named the Cojuangcos rather than being indorsed in blank, the familiar Marcos modus operandi was absent and Cojuangco had been the beneficial owner from the start.
